extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, marketing researchers, and graduate students studying humor theory and experimental emotion research
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of what makes stimuli (videos, product descriptions, sports plays) humorous, comparing alternative conceptualizations of incongruity (surprise, juxtaposition, atypicality, resolution) and testing the benign violation hypothesis (joint presence of violation appraisal and benign appraisal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceiving the event as worse than what is normally expected (a failure or outcome that deviates negatively from expectation). Measured with items like “The outcome of the pole vault was not ideal” and “The pole vault attempt failed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violation appraisal positively predicts perceived humor when controlling for surprise and concern. Not all violations elicit humor (harmful failures were less humorous than harmless failures). For products, items include “is different from what I think products should be like,” “seems like a bad idea,” and “shouldn’t exist” (multi-item scale, alpha ≈ .90).

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign appraisal (benignness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appraising a violation as harmless, inconsequential, or not worrisome for the target; operationalized by participant concern about the person/norm threatened by the violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured with items such as “I was worried about the athlete in the video” and “I was concerned for the athlete’s well‑being” (higher concern → lower likelihood of benign appraisal). The benign appraisal (low concern / perception of harmlessness) is necessary, jointly with violation appraisal, to predict humor (i.e., benign violations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign violation (joint condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs when an event is appraised both as a violation (something is wrong/bad/abnormal) and as benign (harmless or acceptable) — i.e., the joint presence of violation appraisal and benign appraisal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across experiments, the joint presence of a violation appraisal and a benign appraisal better differentiated humorous from non-humorous stimuli than violation alone, surprise, juxtaposition, atypicality, or resolved incongruity. Examples: harmless failure elicited more humor than harmful failure or success; products combining juxtaposition and violation elicited more humor than juxtaposition alone; humorous videos were more likely to be perceived as benign violations than frightening or inspiring videos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (incongruity-as-surprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalizing incongruity as surprise or unexpectedness (e.g., items “is surprising” and “is unexpected”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise was not significantly associated with perceived humor in several studies; surprise alone is neither necessary nor sufficient for humor. Also, resolved surprise (incongruity-resolution formulated as surprise being resolved) did not reliably distinguish humorous from non-humorous videos. The authors conclude surprise-based incongruity theories cannot adequately distinguish humorous from non-humorous stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition (incongruity-as-juxtaposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity defined as a juxtaposition of two perceptions, ideas, or features that do not normally fit together (e.g., product that combines attributes that don't typically go together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juxtaposition alone is not sufficient to produce humor — many juxtaposed products are considered innovative/useful rather than funny. Juxtaposition combined with a violation (i.e., juxtaposition + violation) increases perceptions of humor. Measured with items like “juxtaposes different features” and “combines attributes that don’t normally go together” (r ≈ .73).

rubrics_metrics.name: Atypicality (incongruity-as-atypicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity conceptualized as something being atypical, unusual, or abnormal (items: “is atypical,” “is unusual”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atypicality is too broad: many amazing or tragic events are atypical but not humorous. Atypicality may be necessary in some cases but is not sufficient to distinguish humorous from non-humorous events. In regressions, perception of atypicality often failed to predict perceived humor when benign violation was included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-resolution (resolved incongruity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The variant of incongruity theory that humor results from making sense of something that initially seems unexpected or unusual (resolution of surprise or atypicality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution (operationalized as a surprise or atypicality that is subsequently resolved) explains many scripted jokes and advertisements but did not generalize well to videos, sports plays, or everyday humor in these studies; resolved incongruity did not reliably differentiate humorous from frightening or inspiring videos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtaposition that is perceived as benign — i.e., a combination of disparate attributes that does not seem harmful or problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured in Study 5 as a parallel alternative to benign violation (participants selected “There is juxtaposition; it seems benign” vs other options). The study indicates benign juxtaposition alone is insufficient to account for differences between humorous and non-humorous stimuli; juxtaposition is most likely to increase humor when combined with a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern as moderator of benign appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern for the welfare of the person or norm threatened by the violation reduces the likelihood that the violation will be appraised as benign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High concern (measured with worry/concern items) predicts lower perceived humor and is negatively correlated with benign appraisal. Concern is therefore an important covariate to measure when testing benignness and humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement/scaling guidance for constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multi-item scales and specific items to operationalize constructs: humor (e.g., “is humorous,” “is funny,” “makes me laugh”; α ≈ .97), surprise (e.g., “is surprising,” “is unexpected”; r ≈ .69), atypicality (e.g., “is atypical,” “is unusual”; r ≈ .70), juxtaposition (two-item scale; r ≈ .73), violation appraisal (three-item scale; α ≈ .90).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-item measures increase reliability. For some manipulations, dichotomous coding of perceived atypicality/violation/benignness (present vs absent) was used to compare conditions. Provide clear definitions and examples (e.g., sarcasm) to participants to ensure understanding of constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory adequacy criterion (generality vs specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct humor theory must identify conditions that are general enough to be present in humorous events but specific enough not to be present in non-humorous events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper evaluates alternative conceptualizations of incongruity against this standard: many forms of incongruity are too broad (present in terrifying or amazing stimuli as well), whereas benign violation better meets this balance though it is imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization approach for stimuli evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate stimuli by focusing on the most emotional (e.g., most humorous) part and have participants indicate whether there is no incongruity/violation/juxtaposition, an incongruity that is not benign/resolved, or an incongruity that is benign/resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This three-option forced choice (no / yes but not benign / yes and benign or no / yes unresolved / yes resolved) was used across studies to assess presence and resolution/benignness. Counterbalance order of clips and provide definitions before rating; ask participants to paraphrase definitions to ensure comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing harmful vs harmless violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all violations are equally humorous: violations that are harmful (cause concern) are less likely to be perceived as humorous than harmless failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating humorous content, assess whether the violation causes perceived harm or negative consequence; harmful violations reduce humor even if they are violations and surprising/atypical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition × violation interaction for products
rubrics_metrics.description: For consumer products, humor is more likely when product features both juxtaposition (attributes not normally combined) and a violation (combination seems useless or inappropriate) than when it has juxtaposition alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In product description tasks, participants judged product humor higher in the juxtaposition+violation condition than juxtaposition-only or no-juxtaposition. Thus, product design intended to be humorous should produce perceived violation plus a sense of benignness.
